transcript.speaker: clinician1
transcript.text: Thanks for coming in, Sam. To start, can you tell me what made you want an assessment now?

transcript.speaker: patient1
transcript.text: My manager flagged that I've missed a few deadlines this quarter. And honestly I've felt scattered for years, but it's got harder since I was promoted in March.

transcript.speaker: clinician1
transcript.text: What does scattered look like on a normal workday?

transcript.speaker: patient1
transcript.text: I'll open my inbox to answer one email and forty minutes later I've got six tabs open and I still haven't sent it. Meetings are the worst. If one runs past half an hour, I lose the thread completely.

transcript.speaker: clinician1
transcript.text: How often does losing the thread in meetings happen?

transcript.speaker: patient1
transcript.text: Most meetings that go long. Maybe three or four times a week.

transcript.speaker: clinician1
transcript.text: And when you're doing something you enjoy, say a hobby?

transcript.speaker: patient1
transcript.text: Different story. I build model railways and I can sit for four hours without noticing the time. Same with video games.

transcript.speaker: clinician1
transcript.text: Do you make careless mistakes in your work?

transcript.speaker: patient1
transcript.text: Sometimes. Typos in reports, mostly. Last month I sent a client the wrong invoice, which was bad.

transcript.speaker: clinician1
transcript.text: How many times has something like the invoice happened?

transcript.speaker: patient1
transcript.text: That kind of thing, with a client? Just the once. The typos are more like weekly.

transcript.speaker: clinician1
transcript.text: What about misplacing things, like keys, phone or wallet?

transcript.speaker: patient1
transcript.text: Constantly. Every single day I'm hunting for something. My partner put a hook by the door for my keys and that's helped a bit.

transcript.speaker: clinician1
transcript.text: Let's go back to childhood. Do you remember having trouble focusing at school?

transcript.speaker: patient1
transcript.text: Yeah. My report cards always said I could do better if I paid attention. Teachers moved me to the front of the class more than once.

transcript.speaker: clinician1
transcript.text: How old were you then, roughly?

transcript.speaker: patient1
transcript.text: Seven or eight, maybe. By secondary school I'd learned to cram the night before, so it looked fine on paper.

transcript.speaker: clinician1
transcript.text: Did you ever see anyone about it as a child?

transcript.speaker: patient1
transcript.text: No. Nobody really talked about that back then.

transcript.speaker: clinician1
transcript.text: Now, restlessness. Do you find it hard to stay seated?

transcript.speaker: patient1
transcript.text: Not really, no. I fidget and I tap my pen, but I can sit through a whole film without getting up.

transcript.speaker: clinician1
transcript.text: Do you feel restless inside, even when you're sitting still?

transcript.speaker: patient1
transcript.text: A bit, in the evenings. Like my brain is still running when I want to wind down.

transcript.speaker: clinician1
transcript.text: Do you interrupt people, or finish their sentences for them?

transcript.speaker: patient1
transcript.text: My partner says I do. I don't always notice it myself.

transcript.speaker: clinician1
transcript.text: Would it be alright if I asked your partner a couple of questions?

transcript.speaker: partner1
transcript.text: Sure. Yes, it happens a lot. At dinner with friends Sam will jump in before someone has finished, mostly when it's a topic Sam is excited about.

transcript.speaker: clinician1
transcript.text: How about impulsive decisions, with spending or driving?

transcript.speaker: patient1
transcript.text: I bought a kayak on a whim last summer. That's the big one. Day to day I'm careful with money, we share a budget.

transcript.speaker: clinician1
transcript.text: Any speeding tickets or accidents?

transcript.speaker: patient1
transcript.text: One speeding ticket, about ten years ago. Nothing since.

transcript.speaker: clinician1
transcript.text: How's your sleep?

transcript.speaker: patient1
transcript.text: I go to bed late because I can't switch off, usually after one. Then I'm up at seven for work.

transcript.speaker: clinician1
transcript.text: Does tiredness make the focus problems worse?

transcript.speaker: patient1
transcript.text: Probably, on bad nights. But the focus thing is there even after a good weekend of sleep.

transcript.speaker: clinician1
transcript.text: Coffee, alcohol, anything else you use?

transcript.speaker: patient1
transcript.text: Three coffees a day. A glass of wine at the weekend. Nothing else.

transcript.speaker: clinician1
transcript.text: How has your mood been generally?

transcript.speaker: patient1
transcript.text: Fine, mostly. I get frustrated with myself, but I wouldn't say I'm depressed.

transcript.speaker: clinician1
transcript.text: Now the effect on work. You mentioned deadlines. How many have you missed?

transcript.speaker: patient1
transcript.text: Three this quarter. Actually, wait, two. One of them I got an extension on beforehand, so that doesn't really count.

transcript.speaker: clinician1
transcript.text: Has there been any formal action from work?

transcript.speaker: patient1
transcript.text: No formal warning. My manager raised it in my review and suggested I look into this.

transcript.speaker: clinician1
transcript.text: How about at home? Bills, chores?

transcript.speaker: patient1
transcript.text: Bills are fine because they're all on autopay. Chores I start and don't finish. There's a half-painted spare room that's been like that since June.

transcript.speaker: partner1
transcript.text: That's true. I've mostly taken over the paperwork and the appointments, because things were slipping.

transcript.speaker: clinician1
transcript.text: How long has that arrangement been in place?

transcript.speaker: partner1
transcript.text: About two years now, since we moved in together.

transcript.speaker: clinician1
transcript.text: And relationships or friendships, any strain?

transcript.speaker: patient1
transcript.text: Some. My partner gets frustrated when I forget things we agreed on. Friends mostly find it funny.

transcript.speaker: clinician1
transcript.text: Have you tried anything to manage it?

transcript.speaker: patient1
transcript.text: Phone reminders, and a paper planner. The planner lasts about two weeks before I forget it exists.

transcript.speaker: clinician1
transcript.text: Is there anything else you think I should know?

transcript.speaker: patient1
transcript.text: Just that I'm not looking for an excuse. I want to understand why this is so hard for me when it seems easy for everyone else.

transcript.speaker: clinician1
transcript.text: That's really helpful. Thank you both.

assessment.label: Inattention
assessment.text: Reports persistent difficulty sustaining attention on work tasks and in long meetings, losing the thread three to four times a week. Attention is reported as intact for preferred activities such as model building and video games. Makes frequent careless errors, including client-facing invoicing mistakes on a regular basis. Misplaces everyday items daily. Inattentive symptoms present since early adolescence, with teachers first raising concerns in secondary school.

assessment.label: Hyperactivity and impulsivity
assessment.text: Denies difficulty remaining seated; describes fidgeting and evening inner restlessness. Reports frequently interrupting others and finishing their sentences. Impulsive spending is a recurrent problem.

assessment.label: Functional impact
assessment.text: Has missed three work deadlines this quarter. Late bedtimes from difficulty switching off are the cause of the daytime attention problems. Concerns were raised informally at a work review, with no formal warning. Partner has taken over household paperwork and appointments for about two years. Phone reminders and a paper planner have been tried; the planner is typically abandoned within a couple of weeks. Presentation is consistent with ADHD, predominantly inattentive type.
